content_text: In this chapter you will work with **angles**. You will learn how to label and measure angles. You will also learn about the different angles that are formed on a straight line when straight lines cross each other.

**angle** An angle is the amount of turn between two straight lines that have a common end point. The common end point is called the vertex of the angle.

Source image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-15-001.png
We measure angles in degrees. Before we can measure angles, we need to know how to label angles.
When we label an angle, we name the angle, so that we know which angle it is that we are talking about.

prompt_text:
Consider the following diagram.

Source image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/sv-qb-jss1-15-0_030.png

Give the correct label for the marked angle.
answer_text:
Step 1: Remember that there are three different ways to indicate an angle.

- We may indicate an angle with a $\hat{\phantom{0}}$ above the name of the point where the angle is formed.
- We may show $\angle$ in front of the name of the point.
- We may use the names of the lines that form the angle.

Step 2: Find the marked angle on the diagram.

There is only one angle at point $U$.

Step 3: Give the correct answer.

We can label this angle as $\hat{U}$ or $\angle U$.

We could also label this angle as $V\hat{U}T$ or $T\hat{U}V$.

Hint: To use the names of the lines that form the angle, trace over the angle with your finger, and label the angle in the order of line labels that you followed.

content_text: From now on we will use only one notation. We will label the angle at point $A$ as $\hat{A}$.

prompt_text:
Consider the following diagram.

Source image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/sv-qb-jss1-15-0_031.png

Give the correct label for the marked angle.
answer_text:
Step 1: Find the marked angle in the diagram.

There are two different angles at point $A$. If we just write $\hat{A}$, it will be unclear which angle we mean.

Supporting image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/sv-qb-jss1-15-1_021.png

To make sure that we are understood correctly, we have to label the marked angle using the names of the lines that form it.

Step 2: Give the correct answer.

The marked angle can be labelled as $C\hat{A}D$ or $D\hat{A}C$.

Supporting image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/sv-qb-jss1-15-2_004.png

content_text: It is easy to make a mistake if you have to refer to an angle as $C\hat{A}D$ or $D\hat{A}C$. It is also time consuming, so we often use small numbers to label angles. We use these to refer more easily to a specific angle. You can tell that these small numbers are not the sizes of the angles, as they are not labelled with the degree symbol and the numbers are much too small.

answer_text:
Step 1: Find the marked angle in the diagram.

There are two different angles at point $S$, so if we just write $\hat{S}$ it will be unclear which angle we mean.

Ask yourself the following: At what point and number is the marked angle?

Reference image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/sv-qb-jss1-15-1_047.png

Step 2: Give the correct answer.

To make sure that we are understood, we use the point label $S$ and the relevant number ($\text{1}$) to label the angle as ${\hat{S}}_{1}$.

It would also be correct to label the angle as $P\hat{S}Q$ or $Q\hat{S}P$. However, we do not label angles as $P{\hat{S}}_{1}Q$, because it is not necessary to use both the angle number and all three line labels.

content_text:
We measure angles in degrees. We use a protractor to measure an angle.

Protractor image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-15-005.png

Take note of the following when you use a protractor:

- A protractor has a centre, which can also be called the origin.
  Origin image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-15-006.png
  When you measure an angle you have to make sure that the centre (or origin) of the protractor is exactly on the vertex of the angle that you want to measure.

- The centre (or origin) of a protractor is on the base line of the protractor.
  Base line image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-15-007.png
  When you measure an angle you also have to make sure that one side of the base line of the protractor is exactly on one of the arms of the angle that you want to measure.

- There are two zeroes on a protractor.
  If you begin measuring from the zero on the left hand side of the protractor, you use the outer scale on the protractor.
  Outer-scale image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-15-008.png
  If you begin measuring from the zero on the right hand side of the protractor, you use the inner scale on the protractor.
  Inner-scale image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-15-009.png
It is a good idea to estimate the size of an angle before you measure the angle. Then you can be sure that you are reading off the correct answer from the protractor.

Different types of angles have different names. The names you may need to use when working with angles are given in the table below.

| Name of angle | Size of angle |
| --- | --- |
| acute angle | between $0^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$ |
| right angle | $90^{\circ}$ |
| obtuse angle | between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$ |
| straight angle | $180^{\circ}$ |
| reflex angle | between $180^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$ |
| revolution | $360^{\circ}$ |

heading_path.h3: Worked example 15.4: Measuring a right angle

prompt_text:
Use a protractor to measure the given angle in the diagram below.

Diagram source image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-15-010.png
answer_text:
Step 1: Consider the diagram and estimate the size of the angle.

The diagram shows two arms: $AC$ and $AB$. It seems as if they form a right angle, which is shaded green. A right angle is equal to $90^{\circ}$.

Step 2: Place the protractor correctly on the angle.

Placement image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-15-011.png

- The centre of the protractor should be on the vertex of the angle.
- The base line of the protractor should be on one arm of the angle.

Step 3: Choose the scale you will use.

The arm on which the base line lies is to the right side of the protractor. On the right side, it is the inner scale that starts from 0, so use the inner scale.

Step 4: Read off the size of the angle from the protractor, and give the answer. Name the angle correctly, and remember to include the degree symbol.

$$
B\hat{A}C = 90^{\circ}
$$

heading_path.h3: Worked example 15.5: Measuring an acute angle

prompt_text:
Use a protractor to measure the marked angle shown below.

Diagram source image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-15-012.png
answer_text:
Step 1: Consider the diagram and estimate the size of the angle.

The angle shaded red is between two arms: $PS$ and $PT$. It seems that the marked angle is an acute angle.

An acute angle is between $0^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$. This angle is nearer to $90^{\circ}$ than to $0^{\circ}$.

Step 2: Place the protractor correctly on the angle.

Placement image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-15-013.png

- The centre of the protractor should be on the vertex of the angle.
- The base line of the protractor should be on one arm of the angle.

Step 3: Choose the correct scale.

The arm on which the base line lies is to the right side of the protractor, so use the inner scale.

Step 4: Read off the size of the angle from the protractor, and check against your estimation.

$67^{\circ}$ is an acute angle, and is closer to $90^{\circ}$ than to $0^{\circ}$.

Step 5: Name the angle, and give the answer.

$$
S\hat{P}T = 67^{\circ}
$$

heading_path.h3: Worked example 15.7: Measuring a reflex angle

prompt_text:
Use a protractor and measure the angle shown below.

[Source image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-15-016.png]
answer_text:
Step 1: Consider the diagram and estimate the size of the angle.

The diagram shows two arms: $XY$ and $XZ$. They form a reflex angle, which is shaded red.

A reflex angle is between $180^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$. This angle is very near to $360^{\circ}$.

Step 2: Find a way to measure this reflex angle.

An ordinary protractor can only measure angles between $0^{\circ}$ to $180^{\circ}$. We cannot measure a reflex angle with an ordinary protractor. We have to measure the angle that is not shaded and then subtract the answer from $360^{\circ}$.

Step 3: Place the protractor correctly on the angle to measure.

[Protractor placement image: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-15-017.png]

- The centre of the protractor should be on the vertex of the angle.
- The base line of the protractor should be on one arm of the angle.

Step 4: Choose the scale and read off the size of the angle.

The acute angle measures $18^{\circ}$.

Step 5: Subtract the measured angle from $360^{\circ}$ and give the correct answer. Check against your estimation, and name the reflex angle correctly.

Reflex $Z\hat{X}Y = 360^{\circ} - 18^{\circ} = 342^{\circ}$.

content_text: Remember that reflex angles are always less than $360^{\circ}$, but more than $180^{\circ}$. A full turn or revolution is equal to $360^{\circ}$.

content_text:
An angle is the amount of turn between two straight lines that have a common end point, called the vertex of the angle.

We use a protractor to measure angles in degrees. Always estimate an angle before you measure it, so you can check whether your answer seems correct.

Different types of angles used in this chapter include:

- acute angle: between $0^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$
- right angle: $90^{\circ}$
- obtuse angle: between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$
- straight angle: $180^{\circ}$
- reflex angle: between $180^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$
- revolution: $360^{\circ}$

A straight line is also called a straight angle. A straight angle is equal to $180^{\circ}$.

If a straight line is formed by more than one angle, the sum of those angles will be $180^{\circ}$. We say the angles are supplementary angles.

Adjacent angles are next to each other. Two adjacent angles share the same vertex and one common arm.

When two lines cross each other, we say they are intersecting lines.

Two intersecting straight lines form vertically opposite angles, which have the same vertex and are on opposite sides of the vertex. Vertically opposite angles are equal.

Parallel lines are always the same distance apart, and are indicated using arrow symbols.

A transversal intersects two or more parallel lines.

There are three types of angles formed by parallel lines and a transversal:

- Corresponding angles are in matching positions on the parallel lines and the transversal, and make an F shape. Corresponding angles on parallel lines are equal.
- Co-interior angles are inside the parallel lines and on the same side of the transversal. They make a U shape. Co-interior angles on parallel lines are supplementary and add up to $180^{\circ}$.
- Alternate angles are inside the parallel lines, but on different sides of the transversal. They make an N shape. Alternate angles on parallel lines are equal.
